title: Holding deposits, tenancy deposits and permitted fees: what you can be asked to pay when renting in England
summary: What landlords and agents in England can charge: a holding deposit of up to 1 week's rent, a tenancy deposit of up to 5 or 6 weeks' rent that must be protected within 30 days, no rent before signing, rent in advance of up to 1 month after signing, and what to do about a fee that is not allowed. Checked on 15 November 2026.
content:
# Holding deposits, tenancy deposits and permitted fees: what you can be asked to pay when renting in England

Last updated: 2026-11-21

> **Checked on: 15 November 2026.** For renting through a **letting agent** in **England**. "Landlord" here also means the letting agent. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-landlord-includes-agent) For the whole process, see "Renting through a letting agent in England: the full process from search to signing".

## 1. The only payments that are allowed

Landlords and agents can only ask you for these kinds of payment: [See the official source](#guide-evidence-permitted-list)

- rent (once you have signed the tenancy agreement)
- a refundable tenancy deposit
- a refundable holding deposit
- a payment to change the tenancy when you ask
- a payment when you leave without giving enough notice
- payments towards utility bills and communication services
- a fee for late payment of rent
- a fee for replacing a key or security device
- damages for breach of contract

Anything not on this list is a **prohibited payment**. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-refuse-prohibited)

## 2. Holding deposit

- Up to **1 week's rent**, to reserve the property while the landlord carries out checks. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-holding-cap)
- The landlord can normally hold it for 15 days, unless you agree a longer or shorter period in writing. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-holding-15-days)
- You should normally get it back; it can only be kept in cases such as false information, changing your mind, not replying to requests, or failing a Right to Rent check. If it is kept, the landlord must tell you why in writing within 7 days; if it is returned, that must also happen within 7 days, or with your agreement it can go towards your first month's rent or the tenancy deposit. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-holding-return)
- Before paying a holding deposit, read the tenancy agreement and make sure you know which deposits you will need to pay. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-read-before-holding)

For holding deposit rules linked to checks, see "Tenant referencing: identity, income, credit and rental history".

## 3. Rent: none before signing, up to 1 month in advance after

Before you sign the tenancy agreement, the landlord cannot ask for, encourage or accept rent. After signing, you can be asked for up to **1 month's** rent in advance. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-rent-in-advance)

## 4. Tenancy deposit

- If the annual rent is below £50,000, the deposit can be up to **5 weeks' rent**; if it is between £50,000 and £100,000, up to **6 weeks' rent**. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-deposit-cap)
- The landlord or letting agent must put the deposit in a government-approved scheme (the Deposit Protection Service, MyDeposits or the Tenancy Deposit Scheme) **within 30 days** of receiving it. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-deposit-protection)
- Within the same 30 days, the landlord must tell you which scheme protects it, how to get it back, what to do if there is a dispute, and similar information. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-prescribed-info)
- A holding deposit becomes a deposit once you become a tenant, and must then be protected too. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-holding-becomes-deposit)
- At the end of the tenancy, the landlord must return the deposit within 10 days of you both agreeing how much you get back. If you disagree, the scheme offers a free dispute resolution service. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-deposit-return)[See the official source](#guide-evidence-deposit-dispute)

## 5. Other permitted fees

- **Changing the tenancy** (for example adding or removing a person): up to £50, or more if the work costs more; you can ask for proof of the higher cost. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-change-fee)
- **Leaving without enough notice**: no more than the rent due until the minimum notice period would have ended. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-early-leave)
- **Late rent**: interest can only be charged once rent is at least 2 weeks overdue, at no more than 3% above the Bank of England base rate. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-late-rent)
- **Lost keys**: the cost of replacement, with written evidence that it is reasonable. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-keys)
- Default fees must be written into the tenancy agreement. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-default-in-agreement)

## 6. Things you cannot be made to pay for

- The landlord cannot require a regular cleaning fee or a professional clean when you move out; but you must return the property in the same condition as when you moved in, allowing for normal wear and tear. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-cleaning)
- Guarantor companies, contents insurance, deposit replacement products and inventory services: you can choose to use them, but the landlord or agent **cannot make you pay for them**. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-optional-products)

## 7. If you are asked for a fee that is not allowed

1. Refuse to pay and keep evidence; if you have already paid, ask for the money back and keep a record of the reply. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-refuse-prohibited)
2. Contact your local council, which can investigate, help you get the money back and fine the landlord. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-council-prohibited)
3. You can also apply to the First-tier Tribunal (a court that deals with housing issues) for an order to repay it. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-tribunal)
4. If it was a letting agent, you can also report them to their redress scheme: The Property Ombudsman or Property Redress. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-agent-schemes)

Keep receipts and transfer records for everything you pay. [See the official source](#guide-evidence-receipts)

## Check who holds your tenancy deposit
In a custodial scheme, the scheme holds the money. In an insured scheme the landlord or agent usually keeps it during the tenancy and the scheme has rules for disputed money. Both are forms of protection. Save the landlord’s prescribed information, the certificate or reference, and your payment receipt. [Scheme types](#guide-evidence-deposit-models)

If you cannot find the record, ask the landlord or agent in writing. Check with each of the three approved schemes using the address and the names recorded on the tenancy. Keep written replies and get housing advice before any court claim if protection was required but appears to be missing. For a dispute at the end, see [getting your deposit back](/en/renting/renting-moving-out-deposit). [GOV.UK deposit checks](#guide-evidence-deposit-check)

**Elsewhere in the UK:** Wales has its own rules and a one-week holding deposit cap. Scotland caps the tenancy deposit at two months’ rent. Northern Ireland has a separate protection scheme framework. Check the local rules before paying. [Wales](#guide-evidence-deposit-wales) · [Scotland](#guide-evidence-deposit-scotland) · [Northern Ireland](#guide-evidence-deposit-ni)

## Official and authoritative sources

- GOV.UK — Tenant Fees Act 2019: guidance for tenants — https://www.gov.uk/guidance/tenant-fees-act-2019-guidance-for-tenants
- GOV.UK — Renters’ Rights Act overview for tenants — https://www.gov.uk/guidance/renters-rights-act-overview-for-tenants
- GOV.UK — Tenancy deposit protection — https://www.gov.uk/tenancy-deposit-protection
- Shelter England — How to rent: protect yourself when handing over money — https://england.shelter.org.uk/housing_advice/private_renting/how_to_rent_from_a_private_landlord_or_letting_agent/handing_over_money

The sources above were accessed on 15 November 2026.

Last updated: 15 November 2026. This is general information, not legal advice, and it has not been reviewed by a lawyer; if the rules change, GOV.UK and the relevant law take precedence.
